subject: no-code-automation
question: Are leads distributed evenly across the three reps?

artifact.workflow:
Lead assignment workflow:
  Step 1: Set variable counter = 0
  Step 2: rep = reps[counter % 3]   (Asha, Ben, Chen)
  Step 3: Assign lead to rep; counter = counter + 1
AI: "Leads are distributed evenly across the three reps."

ai_claim: Yes. The counter increases after each assignment and cycles through the three reps, so leads are spread evenly.

ai_solution.text: counter starts at 0.
Each lead goes to reps[counter % 3].
counter increases after each lead.
So assignments cycle Asha, Ben, Chen.

failure.misconception: Keeping state in a variable that resets every run
failure.explanation: Each lead triggers a separate run, and step 1 sets counter = 0 at the start of every run. The increment is lost when the run ends, so counter % 3 is always 0 and every lead goes to Asha. Store the counter in persistent storage (a data store, sheet cell or CRM field) and increment it atomically.
failure.why_convincing: Within one run the logic is correct, which makes the cycle look right.

canonical_solution: No: the counter resets each run, so every lead goes to Asha. Keep the counter in persistent storage.

valid_evidence.summary: lead 1: counter 0 -> Asha; lead 2: new run, counter 0 -> Asha; lead 3: counter 0 -> Asha
Run variables do not persist between runs; shared state needs a data store.

hints.text: Ask whether the counter survives between runs.
Step 1 resets it each time.
Variables are scoped to a single run.
Trace three leads.
Step 1 is wrong: the counter resets every run. Persist it.

repair: Store the counter in a data store and read-increment-write it each run.
debrief: Workflows are stateless between runs unless you add storage. Anything that must remember needs a place to live.

subject: no-code-automation
question: Will the CRM have one record per prospect?

artifact.workflow:
Trigger: new demo request (name, email, company)
Action: Create contact in CRM.
Many prospects request demos more than once.
AI: "The CRM will have one clean record per prospect."

ai_claim: Yes. Each prospect is a contact, and the workflow creates contacts, so each prospect has one record.

ai_solution.text: Each prospect submits a demo request.
The workflow creates a contact.
Each prospect becomes a contact.
So there is one record per prospect.

failure.misconception: Creating records without checking for existing ones
failure.explanation: Each submission creates a new contact, so a prospect who requests twice gets two records, splitting their history and confusing sales. Search by email first and update the existing contact (or use the CRM's upsert/'create or update' action).
failure.why_convincing: With one test submission per person, duplicates never appear.

canonical_solution: No: repeat requests create duplicate contacts. Search by email and update, or use an upsert action.

valid_evidence.summary: Two demo requests from ravi@corp.example create two contacts.
Use search-before-create or upsert keyed on a unique field.

counterexamples: Sales reps call the same prospect twice from different records.

hints.text: Submit twice with the same email.
Step 2 always creates.
Deduplicate on a unique key such as email.
Look at the CRM after two submissions.
Step 2 is wrong: repeats create duplicates. Upsert instead.

repair: Use 'Find or create' / upsert by email.
debrief: CRMs decay into duplicate chaos one automation at a time. Upserts keep them clean.

subject: no-code-automation
question: Is the admin token not a concern because team members only build sales workflows?

artifact.workflow:
The CRM connection used by the team's workflows was created with the CRM super-admin's API token.
Eleven team members can edit workflows in the automation workspace.
AI: "Team members only build sales workflows, so the admin token is not a concern."

ai_claim: Yes. The workflows only perform sales tasks, so the admin token is only used for those tasks.

ai_solution.text: The workflows handle sales tasks.
They use the CRM connection.
The token is used only for those tasks.
So its admin rights do not matter.

failure.explanation: Anyone who can edit a workflow can add a step using the connection - exporting every contact, deleting records, changing user permissions - with super-admin power and actions logged as the admin. A mistake or a compromised account has maximum impact. Create a dedicated integration user with only the permissions the workflows need, and restrict who can use the connection.
failure.why_convincing: Intended use is limited, so the power seems unused.

canonical_solution: No: every editor effectively holds super-admin rights. Use a least-privilege integration user.

valid_evidence.summary: An editor adds a step 'Export all contacts to CSV' and emails it externally; the CRM logs it as the super-admin.
Integration credentials should have the minimum permissions required.

counterexamples: A workflow edit can delete the whole CRM.

hints.text: Ask what anyone with the connection could do.
Step 3 considers only intended use.
Permissions define possible actions, not intended ones.
Imagine a new step using the connection.
Step 3 is wrong: editors inherit admin power. Use least privilege.

repair: Create a scoped integration user and limit connection access.
debrief: Shared connections share their privileges. Scope them for what automations actually do.

subject: no-code-automation
question: Does the onboarding workflow still start for every won deal?

artifact.workflow:
Filter: continue only if deal stage exactly equals 'Closed Won'
Last week, sales ops renamed the stage to 'Won - Contract Signed'.
AI: "The onboarding workflow still starts for every won deal."

ai_claim: Yes. Won deals still reach the won stage, so the filter still lets them through.

ai_solution.text: Deals still move to the won stage.
The filter checks for the won stage.
So won deals pass the filter.
Onboarding still starts.

failure.misconception: Depending on a display name that can change
failure.explanation: The filter compares the text 'Closed Won', which no longer matches 'Won - Contract Signed'. Every won deal now fails the filter and onboarding silently stops. Filter on the stage's stable internal ID (or a boolean like is_won), and add monitoring for runs that stop unexpectedly.
failure.why_convincing: The concept of 'won' has not changed.

canonical_solution: No: the text match fails after the rename. Filter on the stage ID or an is_won flag.

valid_evidence.summary: deal moves to 'Won - Contract Signed' -> filter 'equals Closed Won' fails -> no onboarding
Match on stable identifiers, not editable labels.

counterexamples: New customers get no onboarding after the rename.

hints.text: Compare the filter text with the new stage name.
Step 2 assumes the name still matches.
Labels change; IDs do not.
Move a test deal to the new stage.
Step 2 is wrong: the rename breaks the text match. Use the stage ID.

repair: Filter on the stage ID or an is_won field; alert when daily runs drop to zero.
debrief: Business users rename things. Automations should key on identifiers they cannot see.

subject: no-code-automation
question: Is the AI right that this sync picks up every change without re-copying everything or losing updates on failure?

artifact.workflow: Every 10 minutes: fetch CRM deals where updated_at > {{last_cursor}} (sorted by updated_at, paginated), write them to the warehouse (upsert by deal ID), then save the largest updated_at seen as the new last_cursor - only after all writes succeed.

ai_claim: Yes. Only deals changed since the cursor are fetched, upserts avoid duplicates, and because the cursor advances only after successful writes, a failed run re-fetches the same changes next time.

ai_solution.text: The query fetches only records updated after the cursor.
Pagination retrieves all of them.
Upserts by deal ID make re-processing harmless.
Advancing the cursor after success means failures are retried.

canonical_solution: Correct. Cursor-based incremental sync with idempotent writes and commit-after-success is robust. (Using >= with dedupe guards against records sharing the exact cursor timestamp.)

valid_evidence.summary: run fails after writing 40 of 90 deals -> cursor unchanged -> next run re-fetches all 90 -> upserts leave no duplicates

hints.text: Trace a run that fails halfway.
Step 4 is the key ordering.
Commit progress only after the work succeeds.
Consider records written twice.
This solution is correct. The sync is incremental and recoverable. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Incremental syncs need three things: a cursor, idempotent writes, and moving the cursor only after success.
